channel.title: The Dig — Control electronics and cryogenics
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Control electronics and cryogenics preset. Today's ranked reading list leads with 2611.22315, a connectivity-aware transpiler that selects routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis and reports 0.62x the two-qubit gates of Qiskit O3 across 55 benchmarks, and 2611.21270, whose Schmidt-time surrogate and QOC-guided search target pulse-level compilation latency under nearest-neighbor XY coupling; both are directly relevant to compiling for a small, sparsely connected spin-qubit QPU. The skim tier then covers 2611.21578 on temporally correlated leakage and cycle-dependent error accumulation for QEC benchmarking and mitigation, 2611.22260 on circuit-level geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased noise, 2611.23009 on dual-rail logical-physical boundary compilation with delayed realization binding, 2611.22166 on a common-clock superconducting qubit control scheme, and 2611.21397 on quantitative millikelvin microwave power measurement for cryogenic control-line calibration. No pay dirt today — 2 to skim.

item.title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
item.description:
Skim new method — Bipolar high-speed pulse sequences generated from low-frequency guiding waveforms on a single 25 GSa/s common clock achieve 40 ns single-qubit average gate fidelity of 99.94% and 120 ns CZ gate fidelity of (99.63 ± 0.02)%.

Grade 0.562 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems” · Chenyin Sun, Yu Xu, Zihua Chen, Dayu Li, Tianzuo Sun, Chen Zha, Yuan Li, Jin Lin, Lei Jiang, Tao Rong, Tao Jiang, Shaoyu Zhan, Xueshen Wang, Shijian Wang, Wenhui Cao, Yeru Wang, Xiaomin Wang, Ming Gong, Yulin Wu, Yuhuai Li, Gang Wu, Hui Deng, Kai Yan, Sirui Cao, Futian Liang, Fusheng Chen, Qingling Zhu, Yangsen Ye, Hao Rong, Shaojun Guo, Haoran Qian, Haibin Zhang, Yisen Hu, Shaowei Li, Jinjin Li, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Xiaobo Zhu, Jian-Wei Pan

Figure

CZ gate calibration and performance: panels show coupler parameter calibrations versus threshold and guiding frequency, plus cycle-dependent cross-entropy benchmarking fidelity decay.

Asks

Can superconducting qubit single- and two-qubit gates be driven with high fidelity using common-clock digital pulse sequences without per-qubit analog microwave trigger sources?

But

Demonstrated using room-temperature AWG emulation rather than integrated cryogenic SFQ circuits; CZ fidelity standard error omits single-qubit reference error uncertainty.

Tools

guiding-waveform pulse encoding · arbitrary waveform generator at 25 GSa/s · cross-entropy benchmarking · tunable coupler transmon architecture

Abstract

Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns R(φ, fracπ2) gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.

item.title: Quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures: Comparison between dispersively and directly coupled superconducting qubits
item.description:
Skim new result — Cryostat input line attenuation at 6.0 GHz is measured as (74.7±0.2) dB using directly coupled transmons and (75.4±6.8) dB using dispersively coupled transmons. Directly coupled qubits sense from −155 dBm to −130 dBm; dispersively coupled qubits access −95 dBm to −55 dBm.

Grade 0.555 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems”

Figure

Line attenuation estimates and uncertainties determined for three directly coupled transmons and three dispersively coupled transmons at 6.0 GHz and near flux sweet spots (6.8–8.0 GHz).

Asks

Can the AC Stark shift on dispersively coupled transmons achieve quantitative microwave power sensing at millikelvin temperatures, and how does its accuracy compare with resonant wave scattering on directly coupled transmons?

But

Direct coupling requires the qubit to be tuned into resonance with the signal. Dispersive coupling uncertainty is dominated by numerical modeling errors of the feedline-to-resonator transfer function.

Tools

transmon qubits with asymmetric dc-SQUIDs · continuous-wave microwave spectroscopy · electromagnetic and circuit co-simulation (Sonnet and uSimmics) · dilution refrigerator at 20 mK

Abstract

The Rabi frequency of a two-level system is directly proportional to the electric field amplitude being incident on this system. Taking advantage of this relationship, it is possible to use two-level systems as quantitative sensors of electric fields. Here, we apply this concept to superconducting qubits and use them for quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures. Our superconducting circuit design includes three transmon qubits directly coupled to the central microwave feedline and three transmon qubits coupled dispersively via readout resonators to the feedline. We compare both coupling schemes to assess their reliability for microwave power sensing. Further, we describe the modeling behind each power-sensing method, including an uncertainty estimation based upon repeated measurements. By combining dispersively coupled and directly coupled qubits on the same device, we are able to explore different power ranges: from -155 dBm to -130 dBm for the directly coupled qubits and from -95 dBm to -55 dBm for the dispersively coupled qubits. When determining the microwave-line attenuation for a frequency of 6.0 GHz from room temperature to the millikelvin stage of the cryostat, we obtain best estimates and uncertainties for the directly coupled transmons of (74.7±0.2) dB and for the dispersively coupled transmons of (75.4±6.8) dB. The larger uncertainty of the dispersively coupled qubit measurements indicates that these qubits are less reliable for power sensing than the directly coupled qubits, most likely, due to the additional coupling resonator, whose transfer function is difficult to estimate accurately. Our results constitute the first step towards validation of qubit power sensing in dilution fridges, leading towards traceability for cryogenic microwave measurements.
